Q_EC.text: The conversation with my manager was actually something I initiated myself, because I realized pretty early on that trying to hide my anxiety was making everything worse, and it felt more honest (and more sustainable, long-term) to just say "this is something I live with" rather than pretend otherwise. I told them I have generalized anxiety, that it sometimes peaks around deadlines or during periods of intense change, and that I'd found certain accommodations really helpful in previous roles -- things like flexible start times so I can do my morning routine properly, and being able to step away for short breaks when I feel overwhelmed rather than pushing through and making more errors. my manager listened really well, asked a few clarifying questions (which I appreciated, because it meant they were taking it seriously rather than just nodding to move on), and within a week or two we had a small written agreement formalizing the flexibility. They also said that if anything changed I should come back and we'd revisit it, which made me feel like it wasnt a one-time checkbox conversation but something ongoing, and honestly that openness made a bigger difference than the specific accommodations themselves -- it changed how I felt about coming to work every day.

Q_CC.text: I've talked to a few coworkers about it at different points, and honestly the reactions have been pretty varied but mostly positive, which I think says something good about the team culture we've built over time. The first time was a bit unplanned -- a colleague noticed I'd stepped away from a team meeting for a few minutes and when I came back she just quietly asked if I was okay, and something about the way she asked made it feel safe to say more than "yeah I'm fine," so I told her a bit about the anxiety and how sometimes I just need a reset. she was really warm about it, said she had a friend who dealt with something similar, and after that she'd occasionally just send me a low-key message before a high-stakes presentation like "you've got this" which sounds small but genuinely helped. A couple of other conversations have happened more organically over lunch or during slower periods, and I've made a point of being relatively open rather than vague, partly because I think the more people normalize saying "I have anxiety" in a matter-of-fact way, the less it feels like a confession and the more it just feels like information about how you work best -- which is really all it is. There's been one or two people who got a bit awkward, not unkind, just unsure what to say, but even that feels like an opportunity more than a setback, because usually a follow-up conversation clears it up and they relax once they realize I'm not asking for anything dramatic, just a bit of understanding.

Q_CW.text: There's one conversation that stands out quite a bit, and it happened maybe six months into my current role, so we'd gotten to know each other well enough that there was some real trust there already. A colleague came to me after a particularly rough sprint and said they'd been struggling with what they described as "just not being able to switch off" -- the kind of low-level constant dread that I recognized immediately, even though they weren't using clinical language for it. I think they came to me partly because they'd heard me mention my own anxiety in a team meeting once, almost in passing, and I suspect that made me feel like a safer person to approach than, say, a manager. The conversation was pretty long actually, we ended up staying back after everyone else had left, and they were clearly relieved to be talking about it but also nervous about what it meant -- like whether this was "serious enough" to do something about, or whether they were just being dramatic (their words, not mine, and I pushed back on that framing pretty firmly). I shared some of what had worked for me in terms of getting support and also mentioned that our HR team had resources I'd personally found useful, without being prescriptive about it, because I think people need to find their own path. they seemed lighter by the end of it, and since then weve had a kind of informal check-in thing where we'll occasionally just ask each other how the week is actually going -- which I think is a small but genuinely meaningful thing, the kind of connection that makes a workplace feel like more than just a transaction.

Q_PE.text: The conversation with my previous employer was a bit more tentative than what I've experienced since, partly because it was actually the first time I'd ever told an employer directly about my anxiety, so I was still figuring out how much to say and how to frame it without it sounding like a liability rather than just a practical thing to communicate. I remember I kept it fairly brief initially -- I said I had an anxiety condition that occasionally affected my focus and that I was managing it well but that a couple of small adjustments would help me do my best work, and I asked specifically about flexible hours in the morning and the option to work from home one day a week during high-pressure periods. My manager at the time was genuinely kind about it, I want to be clear about that, though I could tell they were a little uncertain about the process -- like they weren't quite sure what they were allowed to offer versus what required HR involvement, so there was a bit of back-and-forth over a few weeks before anything was formalized, which felt a bit drawn out even if I understood why. Eventually HR got involved and we landed on a modified schedule for busy quarters, which worked reasonably well in practice. What I took from that experience was that the goodwill was there but the infrastructure wasn't quite, and honestly that's what made me more proactive with my current employer -- I came in with a clearer ask and a better sense of what I needed, because I'd already gone through the process once and knew what actually helped versus what I thought might help.

Q_PC.text: With previous coworkers it was a slower, more gradual process than what's happened in my current role, partly because at the time I hadn't quite developed the habit of being upfront about it and partly because I wasn't sure yet how the culture would receive it -- and I think those two things feed each other, honestly, because when you're uncertain about the culture you stay quieter, and staying quieter means you never quite get the data to know whether the culture is actually safe or not. The first coworker I told was someone I'd worked closely with on a long project and we'd built up the kind of easy rapport where you end up talking about real things over coffee, and I mentioned it almost incidentally at first, just as context for why I'd seemed a bit off during a particularly chaotic week, and she took it completely in stride, which was a relief. A couple of others I told a bit later, after I'd gotten more comfortable with the language of it, and the reactions were mostly warm even if people didn't always know what to say in the moment (which I've stopped reading as a negative signal, because not knowing what to say is pretty different from not caring). There was one person who responded with a lot of unsolicited advice about diet and exercise, which I found a bit exhausting even though it was well-intentioned, and I think that interaction is part of what made me more deliberate later about how I frame these conversations -- I've learned to say "I'm not really looking for solutions, just wanted you to have the context" right at the start, and it completely changes the dynamic. Overall though, my previous coworkers were decent about it, and I think some of those early conversations were actually good practice for being more open now

Q_CA.text: Honestly, the impact has been more positive than I would have predicted if you'd asked me a few years ago, when I was still pretty guarded about it, and I think that's at least partly because I've been deliberate about who I tell and how I frame it -- not as a weakness or a disclaimer but just as useful information about how I work. I haven't been passed over for anything I'm aware of, and if anything I think being known as someone who talks openly about mental health has occasionally opened doors, in the sense that people come to me when they're struggling or when teams are trying to think through wellbeing stuff more seriously. There's probably some selection bias in my experience -- I've actively sought out workplaces with decent cultures and left ones that felt off -- so I don't want to suggest it's been universally smooth, because I know that's not everyone's story and the structural stigma is real. But for me personally, being identified this way has felt more like a professional asset than a liability, which I'm genuinely grateful for even as I recognize how much of that comes down to luck and circumstance rather than anything I did right.

Q_BH.text: The one that comes to mind most readily is the coworker I mentioned who responded to my disclosure with a lot of unsolicited wellness advice -- this was at my previous workplace and the person genuinely meant well, I want to be clear about that, because I think it matters for understanding why it felt the way it did. I'd told them I had anxiety, kept it relatively low-key, and within about thirty seconds they were telling me I should try cutting caffeine, that exercise really does work if you commit to it, and had I ever looked into meditation apps, and there was something about the speed and certainty of it that felt a bit deflating, like the information I'd shared had immediately been converted into a problem to be solved rather than just... a thing about me that I was sharing as context. I didn't feel unsafe or judged in any hostile sense, but I did feel slightly unseen, which is a different kind of bad in some ways because it's harder to name and harder to push back on without seeming ungrateful. I remember walking away from that conversation feeling more tired than when I started, which is the opposite of what you want from that kind of disclosure. What made it "badly handled" in my mind wasn't malice, it was the assumption that I'd brought it up because I needed fixing -- and I think that's actually a pretty common pattern, people reach for solutions because sitting with someone else's difficulty feels uncomfortable, but the effect on the person disclosing is that you end up feeling like a project rather than a colleague. I've thought about that interaction a fair bit since, mostly because it shaped how I now coach people who come to me after a colleague has disclosed something to them.

Q_SH.text: The one that stands out most, and that I've probably thought about more than any other single interaction in my working life, is the conversation with my current manager after I first disclosed -- not because of any single dramatic gesture but because of a quality of attention that I don't think I'd quite experienced before in a professional context. She didn't immediately offer solutions or reassurances, she just asked questions, and they were specific questions -- "what does a bad day actually look like for you, practically speaking?" and "is there anything that makes it harder that I might not be aware of?" -- which sounds simple but requires the person asking to genuinely set aside their own discomfort long enough to be curious, and that's rarer than it should be. The written accommodation agreement we ended up with was useful in a practical sense, but honestly it was the follow-up -- her checking in a few weeks later to ask how the flexibility was working, whether anything needed adjusting -- that made the difference. It communicated that this wasn't a thing to be processed and filed away, it was an ongoing conversation, and I think that's actually the thing I try to explain when people ask me what "being supported" actually means in practice: its less about the specific thing someone does and more about whether they treat your disclosure as the beginning of something rather than the end of it.

Q_ID.text: The thing I keep coming back to is that most of the good outcomes I've experienced have been the result of individual managers being thoughtful rather than any systemic structure that would have produced the same result regardless of who was managing me, and I think that's actually the core problem -- you can't build a mentally healthy workplace on the goodwill of specific people, because people change roles and leave and get promoted, and what you want is infrastructure that works even when the manager isn't particularly empathetic by nature. So concretely: normalize accommodation requests the same way you normalize any other logistical adjustment, build them into onboarding rather than treating them as a special exception process that requires a brave conversation to even initiate, and train managers not just in what to say but in what not to do -- because a lot of the damage I've seen comes from well-meaning responses that still manage to make people feel like problems. On the stigma side, I think the industry has gotten better at the surface level -- mental health days, EAP programs, the occasional all-hands where someone shares their story -- but those gestures land differently depending on whether the culture underneath them is actually safe, and you can tell pretty quickly when they're performative versus real. what would actually move the needle is senior people talking about their own mental health in contexts that aren't specifically designated "safe spaces" for that, because that's what normalizes it at the level of culture rather than policy. I've seen one senior engineer do this at a previous company and the ripple effect was genuinely remarkable -- suddenly a lot of quieter conversations started happening that hadn't before.

Q_EC.text: Was having a particularly bad anxiety episode that had lasted a few days and was negatively affecting work so I asked if I could take a few days off, and explained why. He said yes, and we now have open communication about my illness and he allows me some "exceptions" from rules. Such as I have more flexible work hours, and I can work from home when I need to. I can take "anxiety days" when I need to. I do take them unpaid since that gives me less anxiety and then it doesn't show on the budget higher up (A large company has a small office in my country and these are all arrangements at that office.) but he is fine with me taking them as paid sick days, again my choice not to do so. All I have to do is inform my team when I'm showing up very late or not at all or working from home, it is such a relief to be able to have honest open communication and has lessened a lot of anxiety that I had about "being sick a lot" or if they thought I was a lazy person. My anxiety also affects my sleep a lot and now since making these adjustments I have not had to show up for work unslept and the even though I have fewer hours some weeks then I did before they are more productive and I'm happier about them. He did ask a lot about if there was anything at work that was making things worse and what they could do better, and when they were changing up teams at my office I was asked before anything was finalized.

Q_EC.text: They knew about the anxiety well before things escalated. When I disclosed the PTSD — and the circumstances behind it — HR moved fairly quickly to separate me from the situation. Q_CC.text: A few close colleagues knew — people I trusted enough to give some context to, mostly so they'd understand if I seemed off or needed to step away from certain situations. One person had their own experience with trauma and that conversation ended up being more mutual than I expected. there was one coworker who got a bit awkward about it afterward, not unkind, just visibly unsure how to act — which I understood, even if it was a little isolating for a while.

Q_CW.text: One colleague opened up to me after I'd shared some of what I was dealing with -- they disclosed something from their own past, a different situation but involving real fear. I could tell it cost them something to say out loud. We ended up talking for longer than I expected, honestly. I just tried to listen and not minimize it.

Q_PE.text: At my previous job I did mention the anxiety — this was before the PTSD, so it was a simpler disclosure. It came up because I was struggling with some travel requirements and needed to explain why. My manager at the time was polite about it, suggested I look into the EAP, and that was more or less the end of it. Not unsupportive, but not really engaged either. I don't think they knew what to do with the information, honestly.

Q_PC.text: At that job I kept it pretty contained — I told one person, a colleague I'd worked closely with for a while, mostly because it explained some things about how I was managing my schedule. She was kind about it, didn't make it a big deal, which was actually what I needed at the time. I don't think I wanted more than that from coworkers then. the anxiety was real but I hadn't yet learned how to talk about it in a way that felt like it was worth the vulnerability, so I kept the circle small.

Q_CA.text: The effects have been mixed, honestly. Giving a public talk on anxiety opened some doors — conversations I might not have had otherwise, colleagues who reached out afterward in ways that felt meaningful. But there have also been moments where I sensed a disclosure had quietly shifted how someone saw me professionally, a subtle recalibration in what they assumed I could handle. I've worked to counteract that through consistent performance, and I think it's largely held — but the concern doesn't fully go away.

Q_BH.text: The one that stays with me is actually from before my current role. When the situation that led to the PTSD was still ongoing, I went to HR at that job and tried to explain that I didn't feel safe — not just stressed, but genuinely unsafe around a specific person. The response was to frame it as an interpersonal conflict and suggest mediation. I wasn't asking to mediate. I was asking to be protected. The instinct to flatten it into a "both sides" workplace dispute, rather than take seriously what I was describing, was the part that did the most damage — it made me feel like I had to prove the threat was real before anything would happen, which is a terrible position to be in when you're already frightened.

Q_SH.text: The response at my current job stands out by comparison. When I finally laid out the full picture — the PTSD, the reason for it, the fact that I'd needed to fear for my physical safety — my manager didn't flinch or try to reframe it. She asked what I needed, and she meant it practically: adjusted deadlines, coverage for some responsibilities while I was getting more acute support, and a standing check-in that was genuinely about how I was doing rather than just whether I was functional. HR in that instance also moved to act rather than investigate whether action was warranted. I think what made it land differently was that no one tried to normalize it or make it smaller than it was. they just took the next step.

Q_ID.text: The biggest gap I've seen is between policy and actual response — most companies have an EAP listed somewhere, but what happens when someone discloses something serious depends almost entirely on the individual manager. Training managers to act rather than just listen would help a lot. And for situations involving genuine safety concerns, HR needs a clearer mandate to respond rather than mediate. the cultural conversation around mental health is improving, but the structural piece honestly hasn't caught up.

Q_EC.text: I told my manager about my clinical depression during a one-on-one, which felt incredibly vulnerable at the time. they were genuinely supportive -- asked what I needed, and adjusted my workload during a really difficult stretch. Honestly, being lauded for my openness rather than penalized for it was not something I expected, but it changed how I think about disclosure at work.

Q_CC.text: A few coworkers already knew because I'd been open about it -- they were kind, mostly, though some clearly weren't sure what to say. One colleague in particular checked in regularly during that stretch, which honestly meant a lot more than I expected.

Q_CW.text: A colleague came to me after I'd been open about my own experience — I think my disclosure made it easier for them to share that they'd been struggling with anxiety for months. they were hesitant at first, kind of circling around it, but eventually just said it outright. I tried to respond the way I'd hoped people would respond to me, which felt like the only thing I could really offer.

Q_PE.text: My previous employer was also supportive, though the response felt a bit more formal -- less personal than what I experienced later. They offered some scheduling flexibility and pointed me toward the EAP, which was genuinely helpful even if the conversation itself felt a little scripted. I didn't feel penalized, which honestly was all I was hoping for at the time.

Q_PC.text: Most of my previous coworkers were pretty warm about it once I opened up -- a couple even said they'd had similar experiences themselves, which felt unexpectedly connecting. There wasn't much awkwardness, though a few people kind of faded into the background after that, not unkindly, just... unsure what to do with it I guess.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, less than I feared it would. There were moments early on where I wondered if I'd made myself too vulnerable, whether certain opportunities had quietly passed me by because of it -- but I can't point to anything concrete. If anything, being open has made me more trusted, not less, at least in the environments I've been in.

Q_BH.text: There was one disclosure that went differently -- when I shared more of the full picture of my mental health history, the reaction shifted noticeably. No overt rejection, but a kind of discomfort that settled in the room and honestly I didn't push past it.

Q_ID.text: Normalize disclosure as a cultural expectation, not just a policy statement -- and invest in training managers to actually respond well, because that moment of reaction honestly matters more than any EAP listing nobody reads.

Q_AE.text: I'd just say that the survey captures a lot of the landscape but maybe underweights how much the specific relationship with a manager shapes everything downstream -- policy matters less than that one person's reaction in the moment, honestly. And for people with more complex histories than depression alone, the stakes of that moment feel a lot higher.

Q_EC.text: The first time I asked for help, my manager thanked me for my transparency and then scheduled a meeting with HR. That meeting ended my employment. The second time — different company — I framed it as a medical accommodation request. Same result. I don't disclose anymore unless there's a written accommodation policy in place first.

Q_CC.text: Coworkers have been different. A few found out through my VA appointment schedule — I had standing medical blocks I couldn't hide, and eventually someone asked. The ones who knew were mostly quiet about it, which I appreciated. a couple were genuinely supportive. I keep it separate from anything involving my employer, though. That line matters.

Q_CW.text: A coworker came to me after noticing the VA blocks on my calendar. they were dealing with depression -- had been for years -- and hadn't told anyone at work. Mostly they needed someone to listen, so I did. I also told them what I'd learned the hard way: get any accommodations in writing before you disclose, and don't assume good faith from HR.

Q_PE.text: I told my supervisor I was struggling — named the conditions, asked about accommodations. He said he appreciated me trusting him with that. Two days later I was in an HR meeting about "performance concerns" that hadn't existed the week before. There was no accommodation. There was a separation agreement. I signed it because I needed the severance.

Q_PC.text: At the first job, word got around after I was let go. A few coworkers reached out to say they were sorry, that they didn't understand what happened. I didn't explain. At the second job I hadn't told any coworkers directly -- the termination came too fast for that to matter. The ones I was close to knew something was wrong but not what. I didnt see the point in filling in the blanks after the fact.

Q_CA.text: It ended two jobs. Directly and quickly. I have no way to prove it was retaliation — the paperwork never says that — but the timing was not ambiguous. I'm more careful now, which means I spend energy managing information instead of doing my work. That's the ongoing cost.

Q_SH.text: The coworkers who found out through the VA calendar blocks handled it well by not making it a thing. They didn't ask follow-up questions or loop in management. One of them quietly rearranged a recurring meeting that conflicted with my appointment window without saying why. That kind of response — practical, low-key, no performance of concern — is honestly what I needed. it didn't fix anything structural, but it made the day-to-day easier.

Q_ID.text: Stop making accommodation requests informal. Every employer should have a written policy with documented outcomes — not a webpage with a hotline number. Anti-retaliation protections exist on paper, but enforcement falls entirely on the employee after they've already been harmed. The industry needs to make it harder to retaliate, not just easier to talk about feelings. those aren't the same thing.

Q_AE.text: I'm a veteran. My conditions are service-connected, and my relationship with disclosure was shaped long before I ever worked in tech -- by a system that documented my mental health issues and stigmatized them at the same time. The problems in this industry aren't unique. But you can't solve retaliation with culture campaigns or mental health days. Someone in HR has to actually say no to a manager. That hasn't happened to me once.

Q_BH.text: The previous job situation -- I'd been visibly struggling to meet deadlines and finally said something to my manager because I felt like I had no other option. And then over the next month or so I just... noticed I was getting cc'd less, left off meeting invites I'd normally be on. Nobody said anything. It was all very polite and very useless.

Q_SH.text: My current creative director -- that situation I mentioned. I came to her during a genuinely hard stretch and she didn't just absorb the information and move on. She actually did something. Reduced my deadline load, checked in the following week, and did it in a way that felt like a colleague rather than HR going through a checklist. "Let me know if you need anything" is not support, it's a door closing politely. Managers need training on what comes NEXT, not just how to listen in the moment. And honestly, the industry needs to stop treating mental health as an HR checkbox and start building it into how teams are actually structured and evaluated.

Q_PE.text: Previous job was a different story. I didn't disclose and honestly I don't think I would've — the culture wasn't there. I just managed it on my own and kind of white-knuckled through the bad stretches.

Q_CA.text: Honestly, at my current job it hasn't really hurt me — if anything being upfront kind of freed me up to actually do my work better. But I'm also aware I got lucky with a decent manager. I think about it sometimes, like whether it would follow me if I switched jobs or if a different employer would see it differently.

Q_BH.text: At the previous job there was one point where I was visibly struggling — missing some deadlines, seemed off — and my manager's response was basically just "are you going to be able to handle this workload or not." No curiosity, no check-in, just performance concern. I never disclosed but I mean, that response kind of confirmed I was right not to. it made me pull back even more.

Q_ID.text: More normalisation honestly — like making mental health part of regular check-ins rather than something people have to bring up themselves. And managers need actual training, not just a one-hour diversity module. The thing that helped me most was just having a manager who didn't make it weird, and that shouldn't be luck of the draw.

Q_AE.text: One thing that doesn't come up much in these surveys — the peer support piece is doing a lot of heavy lifting that employers don't really account for. Like, having that one coworker I could actually talk to probably kept me functional through some rough patches more than any official resource did. that's not really something you can policy your way into, but it's worth knowing that's where a lot of the real support happens. Also, I think there's still a lot of stigma specifically around medication — people are more willing to say "I'm struggling" than "I take antidepressants," and closing that gap feels important.
